kaigo-atomic-bath-environment.heading: Bathing purposes and checks of environment and condition
paragraphs: Bathing and keeping clean remove skin dirt and reduce infection risk, while also supporting feelings of freshness, relaxation and satisfaction and a daily rhythm. Washing does not establish that infection cannot occur; continue necessary infection precautions. Ask what the person finds comfortable rather than making completion of the scheduled bath the sole purpose.

The textbook describes effects associated with bathing: warming the body dilates blood vessels and promotes blood flow and metabolism; muscle and joint pain may ease, making movement easier; and gastrointestinal activity and appetite may be stimulated. Circulation and temperature regulation also change, but effects vary with the person’s condition. Do not present these explanations as promises to treat disease or restore joint function. Check whether bathing is suitable for the person and which method fits.

A sudden temperature difference between the changing room and bathroom puts strain on the body. Excessively hot water also causes strain, so check room and water temperatures separately. A dry floor does not establish that these temperature conditions are safe too.

Inspect slippery floors, steps, routes, support points and assistive equipment. Even familiar equipment needs checking for damage and positioning problems before use. Check the environment and required number of helpers against the person’s mobility and sitting abilities in the individual plan.

Before bathing, check the person’s condition that day and their wishes. Explain the purpose, what will happen and the assistance needed, and obtain consent. The source advises avoiding bathing on an empty stomach or immediately after meals because of effects on digestion and absorption. Check the plan against the person’s meal times and condition; do not change the precaution about bathing straight after a meal merely to suit staff availability.

Check how the person should take fluids before and after bathing according to their condition and plan. Do not recommend the same amount to everyone, including people with drinking restrictions. Prepare clothes and towels in advance and, as far as possible, let the person choose what to wear.

Because the person may feel a need to urinate during bathing, ask beforehand whether they would like to use the toilet. This does not mean forcing everyone to eliminate. Prepare by checking the seat, placement of supplies and which actions the person will perform.

Respect the person’s feelings about exposure and uncover only the area needed for the current care. Explain necessary observation and how screening will be provided. During hygiene care, observe the skin within the agreed scope. If you find redness, pain or wounds, report their location and condition specifically to healthcare professionals.

If the person’s condition changes or conditions prevent safe care, do not force yourself to continue just to complete the schedule. Follow facility procedures to request necessary assistance or contact healthcare professionals. Written knowledge alone is not a basis for performing unfamiliar transfers or bathing assistance.

Learning comparison: the floor is dry, but the changing room is cold and supporting equipment has not been inspected. Do not conclude ‘the floor is dry, so we can start.’ Check temperature, equipment, the person’s condition and assistance requirements before explaining the care.

kaigo-atomic-grooming-purpose.heading: Support personal identity and opportunities to choose through grooming
paragraphs: Grooming includes washing the face, arranging hair, caring for facial hair and nails, changing clothes and oral hygiene. It supports not only cleanliness but also self-expression and relationships with others. Do not apply staff preferences about appearance to everyone.

Clothing helps regulate body temperature and protect the skin. Consider the season, activity, and the person’s body and feelings, and check comfort and ease of movement. Choosing colors and styles from age alone does not identify the person’s preferences.

Ask about valued habits, makeup and hairstyle preferences, and personal values. Supporting continued dressing and grooming actions the person can perform also uses and helps maintain their remaining physical and mental functions. Grooming may support motivation and daily rhythm, but changing clothes does not promise improvement in every physical and mental function.

Even when dressing assistance is needed, ask the person about preferred colors and the order of dressing. Preserve actions they can do and help only where necessary. Receiving physical assistance does not transfer the right to choose to staff.

Before starting grooming, check specifically what may be done and to what extent. Consent to arranging hair does not extend to every change of makeup or clothing. If the person declines one part but wants something else now, ask about these separately.

During assistance, avoid unnecessary exposure and check pain, fatigue and any wish to stop. Afterward, check tightness, wrinkles, comfort and skin changes. Fastening every button does not by itself establish comfort.

Learning comparison: the person wants a blue jacket, while the worker recommends another color because of their age. First ask about personal preferences, and check suitable wearing conditions and today’s activities together. Preserve the opportunity to choose clothes and provide only the support needed for difficult actions.

kaigo-atomic-home-environment.heading: Connect household tasks and surroundings with the person’s life
paragraphs: Household tasks include cooking, cleaning, laundry, organizing clothes and shopping. They relate to instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), and habits and preferences vary greatly. The number of tasks staff complete alone does not establish whether support fits the person’s life.

Cooking connects menu planning, ingredient preparation, cooking, plating and serving, and clearing up. When making meals easier to eat, check condition, illnesses, allergies and personal preferences, and follow the agreed requirements.

Eating provides nutrients needed to sustain life and health. Cooking is part of support that changes ingredients and their ease of eating through methods such as heating and cutting. This does not mean longer cooking enables everyone to absorb nutrients better. Workers must not independently change meal content, texture or treatment-related requirements.

Seasoning and food habits vary between countries and regions, and people from the same region do not all share identical preferences. Seasonal ingredients and festive foods may have personal meaning. New Year osechi dishes are one example, not a rule that everyone should be offered the same foods.

Cleaning removes rubbish, dust and dirt to create a clean, comfortable living space. Also consider the person’s familiar arrangement of belongings and sense of security. Something that seems unnecessary to staff may be important to the person.

Before moving or discarding belongings, confirm what to keep, where items may be moved and what may be discarded, and obtain consent. A request to clean does not authorize freely moving personal items such as glasses. Wheelchair users can also express wishes about their possessions.

Laundry includes sheets and bedding as well as clothing. Check the separate stages: collecting, washing according to materials and care labels, drying and returning to a clean place. An illustration of handwashing or outdoor drying does not make the same method suitable for every material or establish that outdoor drying alone disinfects items.

Items soiled with blood, feces or vomit must not be handled without protection while waiting for an infectious-disease diagnosis. Using standard precautions, check necessary protective equipment, hand hygiene and collection methods. Separate the flow of dirty and clean items, and match handling to facility procedures and risk.

Unnecessarily shaking or spreading soiled linen may spread contamination around the area. Handle it as gently as possible and collect it in designated containers or bags. Do not infer detergent or disinfectant concentrations or washing temperatures from a picture. Check product, material and facility instructions.

Alongside cleanliness, check routes, stairs, access to the bathroom and toilet, slip resistance and handrails. With floor coverings, consider the risk of feet catching on raised or curled edges, looking at both the person’s walking and route condition. The presence of a covering alone does not make a route universally safe or unsafe. Temperature, humidity, ventilation, privacy and emotional security also matter. Use suitable assistive equipment to expand activities the person can do.

Learning comparison: the room is clean, but the call button is out of reach and a worker plans to discard belongings the person wants to keep. Completed cleaning is not enough. Check how the person can call when needed and how they want belongings handled, and arrange the environment accordingly.

kaigo-atomic-dignity.heading: Consider dignity, independence and quality of life in daily living
paragraphs: Needing care does not remove a person’s worth or human rights. The person receives support while remaining the central decision-maker in their own life. Do not impose staff values as the correct answers for them.

QOL means quality of life and includes feelings of satisfaction, happiness and purpose. It is not determined solely by the number of independent actions or health measurements. Ask what the person enjoys and values.

Normalization aims for a society where people with and without disabilities have their human rights protected and can live in their own way within the community. It means addressing prejudice and creating opportunities for mutual support, not making everyone’s actions and preferences identical.

Independence has physical and psychological aspects. Even when someone needs help dressing or moving, respect their thinking and choices about the life they want. Check remaining abilities and personal wishes, and support the parts that need help.

A day includes many actions: waking, dressing, face washing, meals, toileting, walks, tea, bathing and sleep. The textbook’s daily-routine diagram is one example. Use it to understand personal rhythms, not as a rule to make everyone do things at the same times.

Health, household abilities, housing, family and relationships with the community and wider society also affect daily life. Take differences in country, culture, customs and experience into account and check with the person. Do not treat only the lifestyle familiar to staff as the standard.

Receiving support may sometimes make confidence and motivation harder to maintain. However, do not assume everyone who needs care is passive. Find meaningful activities and parts the person wants to do together, and support initiative while checking safety.

Care workers use professional knowledge and skills to support people whose daily lives are affected by aging, disability or other factors. They observe and cooperate with the necessary people to preserve abilities and a personally meaningful life, rather than deciding everything for the person.

Learning comparison: the person needs help putting an arm through a sleeve but wants to choose the jacket’s color. Helping with a movement and taking over the right to choose are separate matters. Confirm the preferred color and discuss help with the difficult part.

kaigo-atomic-privacy-abuse.heading: Protect privacy and respond to suspected abuse
paragraphs: Bathing and toileting can expose body areas the person does not want others to see. Uncover only what the current care requires and cover other areas. Ask about wishes and explain how necessary observations will be made.

Personal information such as age, address, medical history and photographs is not freely shareable just because you learned it through work. Check the need to share, recipient, scope, personal consent and established procedures. Consent to one task does not extend to photographs or another communication method.

Do not assume that omitting names makes it acceptable to post updates on personal social media or send records to private contacts. Share necessary information through designated channels with the designated recipients, and avoid detailed conversations where others can overhear.

Tying limbs, enclosing a bed with rails so the person cannot get out, locking them in, using a belt to prevent standing or excessive medication to suppress behavior can deprive the person of freedom. Consider the purpose and actual restriction, not just the equipment’s name.

Preventing movement can reduce physical function and harm psychological well-being. For people with dementia, anxiety or confusion may increase; restrictions imposed for safety do not necessarily improve their condition. Do not let one worker decide the method alone. Consider restraint-free support as an organization.

Abuse violates the person’s human rights. There are five categories: physical abuse, psychological abuse, neglect, financial abuse and sexual abuse. Understand them through concrete actions such as hitting and injuring, threats or insults, withholding necessary meals or care, improperly using property and sexual acts without consent.

Problems can overlap. For example, withholding meals to make someone obey involves both neglect of necessary care and interactions that cause fear. Selecting one category does not complete the response; protecting the person comes first.

If you learn of words or actions that suggest abuse, secure the person’s safety and record separately the facts you saw or heard, times and the person’s words. Do not wait to provide protection or seek advice until you can establish a legal conclusion yourself. If urgency is high, follow the facility’s emergency procedures to obtain immediate help or medical care.

Alongside internal reporting recipients, check the consultation and reporting contacts, such as the municipality, and procedures appropriate to the suspected abuse. Protecting personal information must not become a reason to prevent necessary safety measures or appropriate reporting. Share the necessary information with the correct contact; this textbook does not replace individual legal judgment.

kaigo-atomic-team-roles.heading: Connect professional roles around the person
paragraphs: A multidisciplinary team uses each profession’s expertise around the life the person wants. Doctors diagnose and treat; nurses provide care during treatment and assist medical practice, among other duties. Assistance with medical practice that requires a doctor’s or dentist’s instructions follows those instructions. Care workers observe and communicate daily changes; they do not independently diagnose or change treatment.

Physical therapists (PTs) work with motor functions such as walking; occupational therapists (OTs) with activities needed for daily life; and speech-language therapists (STs) with functions such as language, hearing and swallowing. These roles work together; one profession does not replace all the others.

Registered dietitians and related professionals consider nutritional balance, required energy and food texture and help develop menus suited to the person. Cooking staff prepare meals according to their responsibilities and confirmed requirements. Care workers specifically report how the person actually ate, amounts and wishes.

Dentists are also healthcare team members, assessing and treating teeth and the mouth. If you observe or hear about denture pain or oral wounds, communicate the location and the person’s complaint for assessment. Care workers do not file dentures to adjust them or provide treatment on their own judgment.

Care managers, social workers and related professionals advise on and coordinate daily life and welfare services and help develop plans supporting their use. They talk with the person and contact family and other parties as necessary. Family views are important information, but do not automatically replace the person’s wishes without checking them.

If eating or swallowing is difficult and today’s food texture is unclear, tell the person responsible what you observed and that instructions remain unconfirmed. Check the assessment and plan with the team, including the responsible nurse, registered dietitian or ST. Workers must not independently change chopping, thickening or energy content.

Completing a coordinated service plan does not prove that services have actually been delivered. Share separately whom you contacted, confirmed conditions and implementation results. Distinguishing observed facts from assumptions supports professional judgment.

Learning comparison: knowing the job title ST does not increase your authority to change the menu for someone with swallowing concerns. Communicate the person’s condition, clarify who will check which instructions and connect them with the support needed.

kaigo-atomic-care-process.heading: Care-service settings and evaluation in the care process
paragraphs: In home-visit services, workers visit the person’s home; in day services, the person attends a facility during the day or similar periods for support. In residential services, they receive support while living at a facility. Check location, timing of use and assistance content rather than treating services as identical based on names alone.

Home-visit care is an example of a visiting service; day care is a day service; and a special nursing home for older people is a residential service. Knowing this classification does not establish that a particular person meets eligibility requirements. Check individual eligibility with the person responsible.

The care process begins with assessment: collecting information about the person and analyzing challenges in daily life. Next, set individual goals and plan specific support, then implement that plan. This process aims to move toward the life the person wants, not merely to fill a staff schedule.

After implementation, check the person’s response and condition, evaluate progress toward goals and whether the plan suited them. The number of times support was provided or the existence of a completed plan does not establish effectiveness or goal achievement.

If evaluation reveals missing information, gather further information or review goals and methods. Assessment, planning, implementation and evaluation are not a one-way procedure that ends; they form a repeating relationship responsive to the person’s life.

Learning comparison: a record claims goal achievement when only the support dates have been set. Actual support, the person’s response and outcomes, and evaluation comparing outcomes with goals are still needed. Check ‘scheduled,’ ‘implemented’ and ‘achieved’ separately.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-environmen.prompt: Does a dry floor establish that all bathing safety conditions are in place?
options: If the floor is dry, water temperature and the person’s condition need not be checked.
If equipment is in place, checking damage and positioning is unnecessary.
No. Also check temperature differences, water temperature, steps, equipment, the person’s condition and required assistance.
If the person wishes to bathe, necessary observation and explanations can be omitted.
rationales: A dry floor is one condition. It does not establish that temperatures or the person’s condition have been checked.
Being installed and being safe and suitable for the person are separate matters.
This checks the environment and the person’s condition from several perspectives to establish suitable support conditions.
Asking about wishes matters, but a wish is not permission to omit necessary explanations or safety conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-grooming-purpos.prompt: The person wants a blue jacket, but a worker thinks only ‘a different color is better for older people.’ Which response is appropriate?
options: The worker chooses a color based on age and tells the person after dressing.
Ask about preferences, check the season, activity and condition, and support the necessary actions.
Because dressing assistance is needed, staff also take over the opportunity to choose the color.
Because the person chose the color, omit checks of comfort and pain.
rationales: An age-based assumption does not respect individuality or choice.
This starts with the person’s wishes and checks actual wearing conditions together with necessary assistance.
Assistance with an action is separate from transferring decision-making rights to staff.
Respecting a choice does not remove the need to check the person’s condition and feelings after dressing.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-home-environmen.prompt: The room is clean, but the person cannot reach the call button and says they do not want their belongings discarded. What is an appropriate response?
options: Record that the living environment is ready because cleaning is complete.
Discard items that seem unnecessary to staff without asking the person.
Omit the reach check because the button’s name has been explained.
Check how the person can call and their wishes about belongings, and arrange safety, security and the agreed scope of consent.
rationales: Even in a clean room, conditions for calling when needed and feeling secure remain unresolved.
The belongings may be important to the person. Check wishes and consent before discarding them.
Explaining a function is not evidence that the person can reach and use it.
This considers usability and the person’s choices as well as cleanliness when arranging the environment.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-dignity.prompt: The person needs help putting on a jacket but wants to choose its color. Which approach supports independence?
options: Because help is needed, staff decide every color too.
If the person can choose a color, do not provide the dressing assistance they need.
Preserve their choices and actions they can do, and support difficult parts.
Use the color another resident chose without asking this person.
rationales: Needing physical help does not remove the person’s right to choose.
Being able to decide and being able to perform every physical action independently are different.
This respects psychological independence and remaining abilities while providing necessary assistance.
Ask the person rather than replacing their wishes with someone else’s preferences.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-privacy-abuse.prompt: You learn that necessary meals are being withheld to make someone obey. Which understanding and response is appropriate?
options: Suspect neglect and psychological harm, protect safety and report observed or heard facts to the appropriate contact.
Meals can be used for discipline, so support does not need to continue.
Provide neither protection nor consultation until you personally establish a legal conclusion.
Because this is an issue between workers, do not record the person’s condition or words.
rationales: This does not overlook withholding necessary meals or interactions causing fear, and connects safety with appropriate consultation and reporting.
Using meals for punishment or control while withholding necessary care is not appropriate support.
Safety measures and consultation are needed even at the stage of suspicion. Do not wait for your own legal conclusion.
Check the effect on the person and record facts separately from their words.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-team-roles.prompt: There are swallowing concerns, and today’s food texture remains unconfirmed. What should a care worker who knows the job title ST do?
options: Knowing the ST’s role permits independently chopping the food finely.
Judge food texture by appearance alone and omit checking the individual plan.
Give everyone the same texture without reporting the person’s condition.
Tell the person responsible what was observed and which instructions remain unconfirmed, and check the professional assessment and current plan.
rationales: Knowing a job title does not authorize changing meal requirements on your own judgment.
Appearance alone cannot confirm whether a texture matches the person’s abilities or instructions.
A uniform approach without checking the person’s condition and individual requirements is inappropriate.
This shares necessary observations and checks with professionals such as the nurse, registered dietitian and ST to connect the person with support.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-care-process.prompt: A record states ‘goal achieved’ when only the support dates have been set. What still needs checking?
options: Only that information was gathered and a plan written.
Implementation of support, the person’s response and outcomes, and evaluation against the goal.
Only the number of scheduled sessions carried out, without checking changes in the person.
Treat evaluation as complete because the goal and support content have been written.
rationales: Information gathering and writing the plan belong to assessment and planning. Goal achievement cannot be evaluated without checking actual support and its outcomes.
Scheduling, implementation, outcomes and evaluation are separate stages. Confirm actual support and the person’s response, then compare real changes with the goal.
The number of sessions provides information about support delivery, but alone does not show the person’s outcomes or progress toward the goal.
Writing goals and specific support is planning. Distinguish this from evaluating suitability and achievement against outcomes after implementation.
